chunks: A number of our companions, from Sahl ibn Ziyad, from Al-Sayyari, from Ibrahim ibn Bustam, from a man from the people of Marv, who said:

Al-Rida (peace be upon him) sent to us while he was with us seeking Al-Suweyq, so we sent him a mixture of Suweyq. He returned it and sent a message to me that Al-Suweyq, when drunk on an empty stomach and it is dry, extinguishes the heat and settles the bile; and when it is mixed, it does not do that.

key_terms.السَّوِيق: Suweyq, a traditional food made from lentils or barley, often prepared as a porridge.
key_terms.الْحَرَارَةَ: Heat, referring to bodily heat or fever in a medical context.
key_terms.الْمِرَّةَ: Bile, referring to the digestive fluid whose balance is considered important in traditional medicine.
key_terms.عَلَى الرِّيقِ: On an empty stomach, literally 'upon the saliva', indicating the state before eating other food.
key_terms.مَلْتُوتٍ: Mixed or blended, referring to the preparation method where ingredients are combined with liquid or other substances.

ai.seo_question: What is the difference between dry and mixed Suweyq according to Imam Al-Rida?
ai.summary: This narration from *Al-Kafi* highlights the Imam’s attention to the physical state of food, distinguishing between the medicinal efficacy of dry, unmoistened *Suweyq* and its diminished effect when mixed. It reflects the Shia scholarly tradition of integrating practical health wisdom with spiritual guidance, emphasizing that specific consumption methods can enhance therapeutic outcomes. The incident underscores the Imam’s role as a guide in both religious and worldly matters, including dietary health.

en.hubeali: A number of our companions, from Sahl Bin Ziyad, from Al Sayyari, from Ibrahim Bin Bustan, form a man from the people of Marv who said,

‘Al-Reza<sup>asws</sup> sent a messenger and he<sup>asws</sup> was seeking Al-Suweyq which was with us. So we sent it over to him<sup>asws</sup> a mixture of Suweyq. So he<sup>asws</sup> returned it and sent a message to us that Al-Suweyq, when it is drunk upon the empty stomach, and it is dry, it extinguished the heat and settles the bile; and when it is mixed, it does not do that’.
en.sarwar: 3. A number of our people have narrated from Sahl ibn Ziyad from al-Sayyariy from Ibrahim ibn Bitam from a man of the people of Marv who has said the following:

“Abu al-Hassan, al-Rida’, ‘Alayhi al-Salam, once sent to us someone asking for sawiq and we sent to him (the Imam) sawiq mixed with ghee or oil. He (the Imam) returned it saying, ‘If one takes dry sawiq before breakfast it dispels temperature, calms down bitterness but when it is mixed it then does not have that effect.’”
